overview: Marlin Global is an NZX-listed, closed-end investment company that gives New Zealand investors diversified, tax-efficient exposure to quality growth companies listed outside New Zealand and Australia (predominantly large-cap US names such as Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Mastercard and Tencent). The portfolio is actively managed by Fisher Funds Management under a high-conviction 'STEEPP' growth-investing process, and the company itself has no employees or operations of its own -- it is simply a listed wrapper around a ~NZ$210m equity portfolio. Marlin listed on the NZX Main Board on 1 November 2007 and is one of three sister Fisher Funds LICs (alongside Kingfish and Barramundi) that share directors and the same fee/warrant/buyback capital-management template.

business_model.summary: Marlin does not generate operating revenue; its 'business' is the total return (capital gains, dividends, interest, less fees/tax and FX hedging effects) on a portfolio of ~26-29 international growth stocks. Shareholder value is a function of (1) the manager's gross investment performance versus its benchmark, (2) the recurring fee drag charged by Fisher Funds, and (3) the discount or premium the market applies to the traded share price versus underlying NAV. Cash is returned via a fixed-formula quarterly dividend (2% of average NAV) funded from realised gains/income, not from any product or service sale.

revenue_streams.name: Realised/unrealised gains on international equity portfolio
Dividend income from portfolio companies
revenue_streams.trend: stable, small relative to capital gains

revenue_streams.name: Interest income on cash balances
revenue_streams.trend: declining as cash held is minimal

revenue_streams.name: FX gains/losses on forward hedging contracts and unhedged currency exposure
revenue_streams.trend: volatile, meaningful swing item in reported income

business_model.customer_type: NZ retail/SMSF-style shareholders seeking a single tax-efficient (PIE-style, foreign investment) vehicle for offshore growth exposure
business_model.geographic_mix: Portfolio ~80% North America, ~13% West Europe, ~4% Asia Pacific, ~3% cash/FFX (as at 30 June 2025); company itself is NZ-domiciled and NZX-listed

main_competitors: Kingfish Limited (Fisher Funds NZ-growth sister LIC)
Barramundi Limited (Fisher Funds Australasian-ex sister LIC, now largely international)
Direct international index ETFs available to NZ investors (e.g. Smartshares/US-listed ETFs)
Other NZX-listed international/global LICs and managed funds
Direct offshore brokerage platforms (Sharesies, Hatch, InteractiveBrokers) offering unwrapped access to the same underlying stocks
competitive_position.market_position: Niche, long-standing (18+ year) closed-end vehicle; small-cap by global standards (~NZ$210-215m NAV) with limited secondary market liquidity; not a market leader, more a legacy structure serving NZ investors who value the PIE/tax wrapper, quarterly income and single-ticket diversification

moat_factors.description: Foreign investment PIE-style structure and consolidated NZX access to offshore growth stocks is administratively simpler than direct offshore investing for many NZ retail investors
Fisher Funds and the STEEPP process have an 18-year performance history and sister-fund scale (Kingfish/Barramundi), but this is a soft moat easily eroded by poor relative performance
Predictable 2% of NAV per quarter distribution appeals to income-seeking NZ retail holders regardless of underlying portfolio return

weaknesses: No structural barrier to entry -- the underlying large-cap US/global stocks are directly accessible to any investor via ETFs or international brokers at far lower cost
Persistent fee drag (1.25% base management fee plus performance fee potential) versus near-zero-cost global index alternatives
Chronic share price discount to NAV (has ranged from double-digit premium to >15% discount over its history) reflecting weak structural demand for closed-end vehicles in the NZ market
Small scale (~NZ$210m) limits liquidity and relevance to larger institutional allocators
Manager underperformed its benchmark badly in FY2025 (gross return +2.7% vs benchmark +14.9%), undermining the core value proposition of active stock-picking

growth_drivers: NAV growth is entirely a function of the manager's stock selection within global growth equities (large-cap US tech/AI, payments, healthcare, consumer, communications)
Active repositioning toward AI-exposed names (Nvidia added FY2025, existing Microsoft/Amazon/Google cloud exposure, Meta/Tencent as AI-driven consumer platforms) as a thematic tailwind

Portfolio broadening -- more positions (26 at FY2025 year-end, up from prior years) across more sectors/geographies intended to reduce single-sector concentration risk (e.g. the FY2025 healthcare drag)
Capital management: buybacks when the discount exceeds 6% and DRP issuance at a 3% discount are designed to narrow the discount and support the share price over time
Any re-rating of the discount toward NAV (or premium, as seen in 2018-2021) would deliver a return uncorrelated with portfolio performance itself

business.description: FY2025 gross performance return of 2.7% badly lagged the 14.9% benchmark due to sector-specific bets (overweight healthcare, zero weight in banks/utilities); high-conviction style produces cyclical multi-year stretches of relative under- and out-performance
Entire investment process depends on Fisher Funds and its senior portfolio manager (Sam Dickie); no in-house alternative if the manager or process changes
Same STEEPP process and overlapping personnel/directors run Kingfish and Barramundi, so idiosyncratic process risk is correlated across the Fisher Funds LIC stable

financial.description: 1.25% p.a. management fee on gross assets (reducible to a 0.75% floor on underperformance) plus a 10% performance fee on returns above the 90-day bank bill +5% hurdle (capped at 1.25% of adjusted NAV) is a structural headwind versus low-cost index alternatives; OPEX ratio ran 1.5-2.2% in recent years

Benchmark is only 50% hedged to NZ$ and Marlin uses forward FX contracts, but FX swings are a material and volatile swing factor in reported gains/losses (e.g. H1-2026 unrealised FX and forward-contract losses of several million dollars)
Fully equity-funded closed-end structure with no borrowings, removing solvency/refinancing risk

regulatory.risk: FMC Act / NZX Main Board compliance costs
regulatory.description: As an FMC reporting entity, ongoing compliance, audit (PwC) and NZX listing costs are a fixed drag on a relatively small asset base
Off-market rebalancing trades between Marlin and other Fisher Funds-managed vehicles require governance oversight to ensure fair, arm's-length pricing

macro.description: Fully invested, unleveraged long-only growth equity portfolio with no downside protection; NAV moves roughly one-for-one with global (especially US) equity market and sector-specific sentiment
FY2025 saw the sharpest US policy-uncertainty readings in decades (tariffs, fiscal deficit, rate volatility) directly driving portfolio volatility and underperformance
Structural overweight in healthcare (28% of portfolio at FY2025) and technology/AI-exposed names (~22%+) creates correlated drawdown risk if either theme reverses

execution.description: Marlin issues a new 1-for-4 warrant annually (most recently record date 22-Apr-2026, exercise 23-Apr-2027, current exercise price $0.87 less dividends declared from 23-Apr-2026); while conversion has historically been low when out-of-the-money (e.g. only 1.0m of 53.7m warrants converted in May 2025), the large overhang (57.3m warrants vs ~227m shares, i.e. ~25% of shares outstanding) creates persistent technical dilution risk and is cited by market commentary as a driver of the widening share price discount in mid-2026

The share price discount to undiluted NAV widened sharply through 2026 -- from roughly a 3% discount/small premium at 30-Jun-2026 to ~9% (14-Jul), ~14% (31-Jul) and ~16% (11-Aug-2026) -- despite an active buyback/DRP capital-management programme, showing the discount can persist or widen even when the stated 6% buyback trigger is active

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global large-cap growth equities (US mega-cap tech, AI infrastructure, payments, healthcare) remain in a volatile but structurally growing phase; NZ-listed international LICs as a category face persistent structural demand weakness versus low-cost ETFs, keeping sector-wide discounts to NAV a recurring feature
macro_factors.cyclicality: High -- NAV and reported profit are directly geared to global (mostly US) equity market cycles with no hedge or downside protection; FY2022 saw a -25.6% adjusted NAV return during the 2022 growth-stock bear market and FY2021 a +40.3% return in the post-COVID recovery
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high indirect sensitivity -- growth/long-duration equities held in the portfolio are rate-sensitive, and the performance fee hurdle and management fee floor are both benchmarked to the NZ 90-Day Bank Bill Index, meaning higher NZ short rates raise the bar the manager must clear to earn a performance fee
macro_factors.currency_exposure: Material and only partially hedged -- benchmark is 50% hedged to NZ$; company uses forward FX contracts (notional ~NZ$105m at 31-Dec-2025) but FX gains/losses on investments and on forward contracts are large, volatile line items in reported income each period
key_input_costs: Management fee (1.25% p.a. of gross assets, reducible to 0.75% floor)
Performance fee (10% of excess return over hurdle, capped at 1.25% of adjusted NAV)
Brokerage/custody/administration fees paid to Fisher Funds and third parties

recent_developments.event: Undiluted NAV $0.8547/share vs share price $0.714 -- discount widened to ~16%, continuing a rapid widening trend through July-August 2026 attributed in market commentary to warrant overhang
Undiluted NAV $0.8003/share vs share price $0.724 -- ~10% discount; five largest holdings Microsoft 7%, Amazon 7%, Meta 6%, Mastercard 6%, Tencent 5%

Board approved new warrant issue (1 warrant for every 4 shares held), record date 22-Apr-2026, quoted from 24-Apr-2026, exercise date expected 23-Apr-2027 at $0.87 less dividends declared from 23-Apr-2026 -- continuing Marlin's annual warrant-issuance capital-management cycle

H1 FY2026 results: net profit after tax $6.462m (6 months to 31-Dec-2025) vs $8.073m pcp; NAV/share $0.94 (30-Jun-2025: $0.95); no buybacks in the half (zero treasury stock on issue); manager did not clear the performance-fee hurdle/HWM so no performance fee accrued
Prior warrant (MLNWG) exercise date -- only 1.0m of a possible 53.7m warrants converted at $0.96 exercise price, reflecting warrants finishing largely out-of-the-money

Disappointing year: gross performance return +2.7% vs benchmark +14.9% (a ~12pp shortfall), net profit fell to just $0.3m from $37.2m in FY2024; management fee rebate of ~$0.44m recorded due to underperformance against the 90-Day Bank Bill Index (fee cut from 1.25% to 1.05% for part of the year)

Manager (Fisher Funds/Sam Dickie) publicly acknowledged process shortcomings after review, added six new positions (including Nvidia, Hermes, Costco, KKR) and exited Dollar General/Dollar Tree, aiming to broaden sector/geography diversification and increase idea-generation cadence

Trump 'Liberation Day' tariff shock triggered a sharp global equity sell-off; manager used the volatility to add to Meta, Intuitive Surgical, Nvidia, KKR and Amazon, and to upgrade quality (Costco, Hermes) funded by trimming lower-conviction names

guidance.as_of: H1 FY2026 Interim Report (16 February 2026) / July 2026 NAV updates

items.target: 2% of average NAV per quarter (formula-based, not a discrete $ guide)
items.notes: Consistently applied policy; FY2025 total was 8.01 cps. Dividend declared 16-Feb-2026 of 1.88 cps, record date 5-Mar-2026, paid 27-Mar-2026. Dividends can include return of capital as well as income/gains.

items.target: Buybacks only when share price discount to NAV exceeds 6% (up to 5% of shares on issue per 12-month period)
items.vs_prior: maintained (threshold lowered from 8% to 6% at some point between FY2022 and FY2025 reports)
items.notes: No buybacks occurred in H1 FY2026 despite the discount widening past 6% in mid-2026 per web-sourced NAV updates, which is a live discrepancy investors should watch for in the FY2026 annual report

items.target: 1-for-4 warrant issued annually; FY2026 warrant record date 22-Apr-2026, exercise date 23-Apr-2027, exercise price $0.87 less dividends declared with record dates 23-Apr-2026 to announcement
items.vs_prior: consistent with prior years' cycle (FY2025 warrant exercise price was $0.96, FY2024 warrant was $1.04)
items.notes: 57,341,670 warrants (MLNWH) on issue as at 21-Jul-2026, representing ~25% of the ~227m ordinary shares -- a large potential dilution overhang if the shares are in-the-money at the April 2027 exercise date

items.target: 1.25% p.a. of gross asset value, floor 0.75% p.a. if performance lags the 90-Day Bank Bill Index by 5pp or more
items.vs_prior: maintained (formula unchanged); actual rate charged fell to 1.05% for part of FY2025/FY2026 due to underperformance-linked rebate mechanism
items.notes: For H1 FY2026 the manager did not underperform sufficiently to trigger a rebate and was invoiced at the full 1.25% rate

guidance.management_commentary: Board and manager commentary (FY2025 Annual Report, dated 10-Sep-2025) acknowledged a 'disappointing' year of underperformance versus benchmark, attributed to overweight healthcare/underweight financials positioning, and outlined process changes (increased new-idea cadence, broader sector/geography diversification, faster response to negative thesis changes) intended to restore consistent outperformance. The board reiterated confidence in the medium-to-long-term investment strategy despite the shortfall, and confirmed the quarterly 2% of NAV dividend policy and ongoing capital management (buyback/DRP/warrant) tools remain unchanged going into FY2026.

bull_case: Access to a professionally managed, diversified portfolio of quality global growth businesses (Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Mastercard, Tencent, Nvidia, etc.) through a single NZX-listed, tax-efficient vehicle, convenient for NZ retail investors

Widening discount to NAV (~10-16% through mid-2026) offers a margin of safety / potential re-rating catalyst if the discount narrows back toward its historical range or the buyback/DRP capital-management tools are used more assertively

Consistent, formulaic quarterly income policy (2% of average NAV per quarter, historically averaging 7-9% p.a. distribution yield) suits income-focused investors regardless of near-term relative portfolio performance

18-year track record and STEEPP process, with an explicit post-FY2025 review and course-correction (broader diversification, faster idea turnover) that could restore the fund's historical outperformance pattern
No leverage/debt on the balance sheet -- a straightforward, fully-invested equity structure with transparent weekly-calculated NAV disclosure
bear_case: FY2025 badly lagged its benchmark (+2.7% gross vs +14.9%), and the underlying stocks (Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Mastercard, Tencent) are directly and far more cheaply accessible via low-cost global index ETFs, undermining the rationale for paying 1.25%+ in fees for active management

Persistent and recently widening share price discount to NAV (from near parity in June 2026 to ~16% by mid-August 2026) shows capital-management tools (buybacks, DRP) have not reliably closed the gap, and the discount itself is a recurring feature of the NZ closed-end LIC sector

Large recurring warrant overhang (57.3m warrants vs ~227m shares, ~25% dilution potential) issued annually is cited by market commentary as a direct contributor to the widening 2026 discount and represents an ongoing, structural dilution risk each cycle

Fully unhedged-to-50%-hedged, unleveraged, long-only growth-equity exposure with no downside protection means NAV can fall sharply in a market drawdown (adjusted NAV return was -25.6% in FY2022) with no offsetting mechanism

Manager-dependency and correlated-process risk across the Fisher Funds LIC stable (Kingfish, Barramundi, Marlin share process/personnel/directors), so a systemic issue with the STEEPP approach or key personnel would likely hit all three vehicles simultaneously
